extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (petitioners and patent owners) and counsel appearing before the PTAB in AIA trials (IPR/PGR/CBM/derivation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for institution, motions, briefing, evidence, hearings, and amendments in AIA trial proceedings before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (IPR/PGR/CBM/derivation).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 325(d) discretionary denial factors (Becton Dickinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-exclusive factors the Board considers in evaluating whether to deny institution under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Becton Dickinson non-exclusive factors include: (1) similarities and material differences between the asserted art and prior art involved during examination; (2) cumulative nature of the asserted art and prior art evaluated during examination; (3) extent to which the asserted art was evaluated during examination; (4) extent of overlap between arguments made during examination and how a petitioner relies on the prior art or a patent owner distinguishes the prior art; (5) whether a petitioner has pointed out sufficiently how the Office erred in evaluating the asserted prior art; and (6) the extent to which additional evidence/facts presented in the petition warrant reconsideration. The Board may also consider materially changed circumstances or evidence not previously before the Office. These factors are non-exclusive and parties may address additional relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of decision on whether to institute (all-or-nothing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When instituting a trial, the Board will either institute as to all claims and all grounds in the petition or institute on no claims and deny institution; it will not institute on fewer than all claims or all challenges in a petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If instituted, the Board generally provides analysis of strengths and weaknesses of all challenges to guide the upcoming trial. The Board retains discretion to deny institution of the petition as a whole under 35 U.S.C. §§ 314(a) and 325(d) even if some challenges meet institution criteria. Where a panel finds only some challenges meet standards, it will evaluate whether, for efficiency and integrity of the patent system, the entire petition should be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling Order and case time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A Scheduling Order will be provided concurrent with institution and will set due dates to ensure trial completion within one year of institution (with limited exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling Order sets Due Dates 1–6 (parties may stipulate changes for Due Dates 1–5 but not extend Due Dates 6 and 7 or requests for oral hearing). Parties may request changes via conference call. The Board aims to complete trials within one year of institution; adjustments may be made for joinder or other circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner response content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: What a patent owner's response must contain when a trial has been instituted for IPR and PGR (and analogous rights in derivation proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The response is an opposition subject to word count limits in 37 C.F.R. § 42.24 and should: identify all involved claims believed patentable and state the basis; include affidavits or factual evidence and explain relevance; may contain a claim chart comparing claim features with evidence. If no response is filed, the patent owner must arrange a conference call to discuss adverse judgment (37 C.F.R. § 42.73(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to amend procedural requirement: confer with Board before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners may file a first motion to amend without prior authorization but must confer with the Board before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121(a), 42.221(a). The patent owner should arrange a conference call or email communication so the panel can provide procedural guidance; early contact is encouraged to incorporate guidance into the motion. Pilot options may permit requesting preliminary guidance or filing a revised motion to amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary burden for substitute claims (Aqua Products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocation of burden of persuasion on patentability of substitute claims presented in a motion to amend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Aqua Products (en banc), the PTO has not adopted a rule placing the burden of persuasion on the patent owner; absent such a rule, the burden ordinarily lies with the petitioner to show proposed substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence. The Board may also justify findings by reference to the record; ultimately the Board determines patentability based on the entire record, including petitioner opposition and any cessation of participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents required in a motion to amend (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121(b), 42.221(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory content requirements for any motion to amend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion must include a claim listing (appendix allowed), clearly show changes being sought, and describe how the original disclosure (and any relied-upon application) supports each added/amended claim. Must identify proposed substitute claim(s) and the original claim they replace, with all changes clearly identified and discussed. Patent owners may not enlarge claim scope or add new matter (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(d)(3), 326(d)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard for substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard the Board will use to interpret claims, including substitute claims, for AIA petitions filed on/after Nov 13, 2018.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will interpret claims using the same standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Final Rule). Patent owner may request a determination that an amended claim is 'substantially identical' to the original claim within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 252 and provide supporting arguments and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of added features and constructions in substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners should identify features added to each substitute claim and any proposed constructions for new claim terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not required, patent owners may provide arguments regarding patentability of substitute claims and may support them with expert testimony explaining what would have been known to a person of ordinary skill and the significance of added features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption on number of substitute claims (reasonable number)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of substitute claims must be 'reasonable' with a presumption that only one substitute claim is needed to replace each challenged claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121(a), 42.221(a). The presumption may be rebutted by showing a demonstrable need for additional substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to amend must respond to a ground of unpatentability
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to amend must respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.121(a)(2)(i). The rule does not require every change to be solely for overcoming an instituted ground; additional modifications addressing §101 or §112 issues, for example, are not precluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor regarding substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have a duty of candor in proceedings, including disclosure of information material to patentability of substitute claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 37 C.F.R. § 42.11, a patent owner must disclose to the Board information it is aware of that is material to the patentability of substitute claims if that information is not already of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments in derivation proceedings (good cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions to amend claims in derivation proceedings are authorized upon a showing of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.20. Examples of good cause include materially advancing settlement or seeking to cancel claims. Requests to cancel all disputed claims may be treated as requests for adverse judgment. Board expects cancellations to be treated accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: General practice tips on amendments (support, timeliness, clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical expectations for motions to amend to increase the likelihood of grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File motions to amend by due dates set for patent owner response, though motions to cancel claims and correcting simple typographical errors may be permitted late. Amendments should clearly state where specification and drawings support all limitations in proposed substitute claims; if the Board cannot determine support, the motion may be denied. Motions must respond to a ground of unpatentability but may include other modifications (e.g., §101 or §112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to a motion to amend (petitioner's rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner may oppose a motion to amend and is afforded an opportunity to fully respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition time is set in the Scheduling Order; no authorization is needed to file opposition. Petitioners may raise new issues arising from proposed substitute claims and may submit new expert declarations or additional prior art directed to the proposed substitute claims. Grounds of unpatentability in response are not limited to 35 U.S.C. § 311(b); the Board may consider §§ 101 and 112 as to proposed substitute claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replies and sur-replies limits (no new evidence or new issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope and limits for replies and sur-replies after patent owner responses and oppositions to motions to amend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner may file a reply to a patent owner response; a patent owner may file a reply to an opposition to a motion to amend. Replies/sur-replies generally may not present new evidence or arguments that could have been presented earlier or raise a new issue (37 C.F.R. § 42.23). Parties may submit rebuttal evidence; if a new expert declaration is submitted, opposing party may cross-examine and move to exclude or comment in sur-reply. Sur-replies normally are authorized by Scheduling Order and may not be accompanied by new evidence other than deposition transcripts from cross-examination of reply witnesses. Examples of impermissible new issues include newly raised rationales to combine references or newly cited prior art intended to 'gap-fill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to submit supplemental information (timing and justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for filing a motion to submit supplemental information after institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.123/42.223: a request for authorization to file supplemental information must be made within one month of institution; supplemental information must be relevant to a claim for which trial has been instituted. To submit information more than one month after institution, a party must request authorization and show why the supplemental information reasonably could not have been obtained earlier and that consideration would be in the interests of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions for joinder (timing, conference call, and discretionary factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: How joinder motions are handled and factors the Board may consider when deciding joinder requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion for joinder should be filed within one month of the date a trial is instituted for the first proceeding (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.122, 42.222). The movant should arrange a conference call with the panel, petitioner, and patent owner of the first proceeding within five business days. Factors considered include why joinder is appropriate, whether a new ground of unpatentability is raised, cost/schedule impact, added complexity to briefing/discovery, time-bar under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b), fairness and prejudice, conduct/gaming of the system, stage and schedule of the existing review, and events in related proceedings. The Board exercises discretion and expects to permit joinder only in limited circumstances where fairness requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment of one-year statutory deadline for joinder
rubrics_metrics.description: How joinder may affect the statutory one-year deadline for issuing a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director/Board may adjust the one-year final decision deadline in cases of joinder (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(a)(11), 326(a)(11); 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.100(c), 42.200(c), 42.300(c)). The Board will endeavor to issue final decisions within one year but may extend (commonly not more than an additional six months) if joinder adds claims/grounds/evidence/arguments that complicate the proceeding. If adjusted, the Board will specify the new deadline in an order before the original one-year period expires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging admissibility of evidence (timing rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: When and how objections to admissibility must be made for deposition evidence and other evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To challenge admissibility of deposition evidence, make an objection during the deposition (37 C.F.R. § 42.64(a)). For evidence other than deposition, file objections within five business days of service of the evidence or ten days after institution of trial (37 C.F.R. § 42.64(b)(1)). Supplemental evidence is served at time of objection and filed only in support of an opposition to a motion to exclude (37 C.F.R. § 42.64(b)(2)). Objections may be preserved only by filing a motion to exclude (37 C.F.R. § 42.64(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to exclude: content and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: How a motion to exclude evidence should be structured and what it may (and may not) be used for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion to exclude should: (a) identify where in the record the objection was originally made; (b) identify where in the record the evidence sought to be excluded was relied upon by an opponent; (c) address objections to exhibits in numerical order; and (d) explain the basis and grounds for each objection (e.g., relevance or hearsay). A motion to exclude must explain why the evidence is not admissible but may not be used to challenge sufficiency of evidence to prove a fact; weight arguments belong in merits documents. The Board often waits until after oral hearing to rule; in some circumstances early resolution may be warranted via pre-hearing conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to strike (standards and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a motion to strike is appropriate and the requested timing for authorization to file one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion to strike may be appropriate when a brief raises new issues, is accompanied by belated evidence, or otherwise exceeds proper scope of reply/sur-reply. Alternatively, authorization to file further merits briefing may be requested. Striking is an exceptional remedy expected to be granted rarely. Authorization to file a motion to strike should generally be requested within one week of the allegedly improper submission; the Board considers such requests case-by-case and will normally decide as soon as practicable, preferably before oral hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing: entitlement, time allotment, and pre-hearing conference
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party is afforded an opportunity to present its case orally; procedures for requesting and preparing for oral hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each party will have at least three Board members hearing the case. Request timing is normally set in the Scheduling Order. A request should state the amount of time sought; Board ordinarily provides an hour per side but parties may request more or less. Parties are encouraged to confer about time allocations. The Board will hold a pre-hearing conference no later than 15 days prior to the hearing to provide guidance on issues the panel wants addressed, identify (but not argue) issues parties want to address, discuss pending motions, and address demonstrative exhibits or unresolved objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrative exhibits at oral hearing (best practices and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on preparation, marking, filing, and permissible use of demonstrative exhibits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elaborate demonstratives often impede argument; effective exhibits are a few presentation slides and a handout/binder. Pages should be numbered and exhibit numbers identified during argument (important for remote panelists). Demonstratives are aids and not evidence and should be clearly marked (e.g., 'DEMONSTRATIVE EXHIBIT – NOT EVIDENCE' on each slide). They cannot advance arguments or introduce evidence not previously presented in the record; doing so may lead to exclusion. Demonstratives should be filed in the record per panel orders; parties should exchange proposed demonstratives and confer to resolve objections. Objections should be carefully framed; Board has found many objections unhelpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live testimony at oral hearing (when permitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for permitting live (in-person) testimony during oral hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live testimony is rare and allowed when the panel believes it will help determination—particularly where witness demeanor is critical to credibility (e.g., inventor antedating a reference) or the testimony is case-dispositive. Requests are considered case-by-case; format is at the panel's discretion. Live testimony is normally evidence that becomes part of the record and the Board may question witnesses. Parties requesting live testimony should explain why demeanor/format matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new evidence or new argument at oral hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations on what may be presented at oral hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At oral hearing, parties may rely on demonstratives and evidence previously submitted but may only present arguments that were relied upon in earlier papers. New arguments or evidence introduced at oral hearing are improper and may be dismissed (see Dell Inc. v. Acceleron; SAS implications). A party may not use oral hearing as a vehicle to present a new prima facie case or newly raised combination rationale.
